nature-econ-100.title: Utility: the economist's yardstick for satisfaction
nature-econ-100.text: Nobody can see satisfaction, yet much of economics is built on measuring it. Utility is the economist's word for how satisfied a person is with a particular state of the world. The idea carries two meanings at once. Normatively, it is a goal to maximize, close to the utilitarian thinking of Bentham and Mill. Descriptively, it is whatever people's choices reveal they are pursuing. A utility function makes this precise by giving each option a number, so that preferred options always score higher. Because utility cannot be observed directly, economists infer it from behavior, for example from how much someone is willing to pay. Paul Samuelson gave these inferred rankings a name, taken up in {{ref:nature-val-094}}. Economists also separate total utility, the satisfaction from a whole bundle of things, from the change that one more unit brings, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-091}}. Maps of equal satisfaction, combined with a spending limit, let economists work out how much people buy at each price. Not everyone is convinced. Joan Robinson called the concept circular: things have utility because people want them, and people wanting them is taken as proof they have utility. Economists and ethicists still disagree about how the normative and descriptive meanings fit together.

nature-econ-119.title: Goods: anything that gives satisfaction
nature-econ-119.text: Air is useful to everyone, yet nobody pays for it. In economics, goods are things that give someone welfare or satisfaction. The subject concentrates on economic goods: those that are scarce because making them takes effort or resources. Things that are not scarce sit outside that circle. The atmosphere and seawater are useful but not scarce enough to carry a money value. Economists sort goods further. Final goods are consumed, while intermediate goods, like transistors, go into making other goods. Durable goods used to produce more goods, such as machinery, human skills or ecosystems, count as capital goods. Goods are commonly assumed to deliver less extra satisfaction with each added unit. Some goods have close stand-ins, so a small price change moves buying a lot. Others, like insulin, have few or none.

nature-econ-134.title: Microeconomics: how people and firms choose
nature-econ-134.text: Economics can be studied one decision at a time. Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies how individuals and firms decide how to use scarce resources, and how their choices interact. It looks at single markets, sectors and industries, while its counterpart, {{ref:nature-econ-541}}, studies the economy as a whole: growth, inflation and unemployment. One goal is to explain how markets set relative prices and share limited resources among competing uses. It shows when markets left to themselves produce desirable outcomes. It also analyzes market failure, when markets fail to deliver efficient results. Its theory usually starts from one rational individual trying to get as much utility as possible. Rational here has a narrow meaning: stable, complete and consistent preferences. Prices, set by the actions of buyers and sellers, sit at its center, so it is also called price theory. Ragnar Frisch likely introduced the split between micro and macro in 1933. The word "microeconomics" first appeared in print in 1941, from Pieter de Wolff.

nature-econ-156.title: Economic value: what something is worth to someone
nature-econ-156.text: Clean air, pollination and flood defense have never carried price tags, yet economists increasingly say they have economic value. Economic value measures the benefit a good or service gives a person, firm or other economic agent. It is usually counted in money, as the most a person is willing and able to pay. At root, value is how much of one wanted thing a person would give up to get another. Early economists split it into value in use and value in exchange, and exchange is what links value to price. Beyond that, agreement breaks down. One theory ties value to the labor needed to make something, while another ties it to the extra satisfaction buyers get from one more unit. Rival theories of value are a major source of disagreement between schools of economics. Many neoclassical theories simply equate value with market price, which has a stark consequence: something with no market to set a price has no economic value. That is why biodiversity's growing economic standing rests on ecosystem services such as clean air, food, water, flood defense and pollination.

nature-econ-089.title: Incentives: what moves people to act
nature-econ-089.text: Pay, praise and the threat of punishment all do the same job: they push behavior in a chosen direction. An incentive is anything that persuades a person or organization to change their behavior toward a desired outcome. Disincentives work the other way, discouraging certain actions. Governments, businesses and other organizations use both constantly. Incentives are often split into intrinsic ones, driven by personal interest or enjoyment, and extrinsic ones, such as pay, recognition or the threat of punishment. Another scheme sorts them into financial, moral and coercive. Trouble starts when parties' goals conflict, creating a misaligned incentive, a problem found in firms and in policy for the environment. Incentives can also produce outcomes nobody intended. Even money is less reliable than it looks. A 2026 study pooling 2,193 estimates from 88 experiments found that financial incentives have a mean effect on performance close to zero in most field settings.

nature-econ-105.title: Ceteris paribus: holding everything else still
nature-econ-105.text: If the price of milk falls, people will buy more milk, ceteris paribus. The Latin phrase means "other things being equal," and it lets economists study the effect of one change while assuming everything else stays the same. It does not claim that nothing else changes. It isolates one cause so its effect can be seen. Alfred Marshall popularized the clause in the 19th century, describing it as a "pound" where disturbing causes are set aside for a time. He also saw its limits. The narrower the question, the less closely it matches real life, as when a model assumes hydrocarbon fuels are infinite. Because economic variables can only be isolated in theory, the method reveals tendencies, not absolutes. In highly interconnected systems, changing one variable changes all the others, so holding the rest constant is impossible in reality.

nature-econ-152.title: Economic models: simple maps of a messy economy
nature-econ-152.text: Economies are shaped by many things at once: decisions, resource limits, environmental and geographical constraints, laws and chance. An economic model cuts through that tangle. It is a simplified, often mathematical, picture of an economic process, built from a set of variables and the relationships between them. Models help forecast economic activity, propose and justify policy, and plan inside firms and centrally planned economies. Some predict only the direction of change, such as buyers wanting less when a price rises, and are often drawn as simple two-dimensional graphs. Most rest on unrealistic assumptions, such as perfect information or frictionless markets. Some leave out important issues such as externalities. Their forecasts can be far apart. In the late 1980s the Brookings Institution compared 12 leading macroeconomic models and found they gave significantly different answers to the same shocks. Like weather forecasts, economic forecasts fail because models cannot capture full detail and are sensitive to small changes in their equations.

nature-econ-141.title: Preferences: how people rank their options
nature-econ-141.text: Taste and need, not price, availability or income, decide what a person wants most. In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted. Most models of decision-making share one basic principle, transitivity: anyone who prefers A to B and B to C should prefer A to C. An ordering that is both transitive and complete is called rational, and people who follow one are called rational agents. Real people do not always behave this way. Their preferences can form cycles with no best choice. Most economic models assume preferences stay stable, an assumption long disputed outside the school described in {{ref:nature-hist-023}}. In fact preferences shift with new technology and social influence, as when friends at lunch shift each other's food choices. Ragnar Frisch built the first mathematical model of preferences for demand and utility theory in 1926.

nature-econ-125.title: Indifference curves: mapping equal satisfaction
nature-econ-125.text: An indifference curve is a line on a graph joining every combination of two goods that a consumer likes equally well. A set of these curves for one person is an indifference map, read like contour lines: curves further out mean more satisfaction. Their downward slope expresses a willingness to give up some of one good for more of the other. They usually bow in toward the origin, the corner of the graph where both amounts are zero. The slope at any point is the rate at which the consumer will make that swap (see {{ref:nature-econ-129}}). The best affordable choice lies where an indifference curve just touches the line of what the consumer can afford. Edgeworth set out the mathematics in 1881, Pareto first drew the curves in 1906, and Hicks and Allen popularized them in the 1930s. Not everyone accepts them. Hovenkamp argued that people value what they own more than what they could buy, so they have no indifference curve at all. Courts, he said, should ask what people would accept to give something up.

nature-econ-108.title: Complementary goods: things that go together
nature-econ-108.text: Razors have been sold cheaply as loss leaders, priced low on purpose to raise demand for the blades. Complementary goods are goods used together, so one becomes more attractive as the other becomes more popular. Cars and gasoline, phones and phone service, and printers and cartridges are everyday pairs. When the price of one falls, people want more of its partner, a link measured by {{ref:nature-econ-368}}, which is negative for such pairs. A perfect complement must be used with its partner, like left and right shoes, and its indifference curve forms a right angle. The bond need not run both ways. A game needs a console, but a console does not need that particular game.

nature-econ-139.title: Ordinal utility: ranking without measuring
nature-econ-139.text: If George prefers A to B and B to C, any set of numbers that keeps that order describes his preferences equally well. The numbers themselves mean nothing. This is ordinal utility: it ranks a person's options in order of preference, saying which is better but not by how much. The alternative, {{ref:nature-econ-101}}, treats the size of the gaps between options as meaningful too. Vilfredo Pareto introduced the ordinal concept in 1906. It turned out to be enough. All of the theory of how consumers choose under certainty can be written in ordinal terms, and usually is. Preferences can be drawn as indifference curves, with curves further from the origin meaning higher utility. For a utility function to exist at all, preferences must be complete, so that any two options can be compared. They must also be transitive: if A beats B and B beats C, A beats C.

nature-econ-140.title: Positive and normative: what is versus what ought to be
nature-econ-140.text: "More government spending would lower unemployment" and "milk should cost $6 a gallon so dairy farmers live better" sound like the same kind of claim. They are not. Positive economics describes and explains how the economy works, so the first statement can in principle be checked against evidence. Normative economics says what people or societies ought to do, so the second rests on value judgments. John Neville Keynes called the first the science of "what is" and the second the study of "what ought to be," and his definitions became standard in teaching. In 1932 Lionel Robbins argued economics should study how to reach given ends with limited resources, not judge which ends to pursue. Some normative work aims to be objective: {{ref:nature-val-001}} seeks the best decision given stated assumptions about value. Ecological economists argue economics is unavoidably normative. The line itself is disputed. Philosophers such as Hilary Putnam doubt that facts and values can be fully separated. Caplan and Miller argue that many supposed disagreements over values are really about facts.

nature-econ-099.title: Trade-offs: more of one thing means less of another
nature-econ-099.text: A full container must lose some items before it can take any more. That is a trade-off in its simplest form: a choice in which you accept less of one thing in return for more of another. Limits of many kinds create trade-offs, even simple physics. Investing shows one clearly. Stocks offer higher potential returns with more risk, while bonds are safer but pay less. Economists express a trade-off as the cost of the most preferred alternative given up, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-095}}. They often draw it as a frontier of the best possible combinations, such as the limit on how much of two goods an economy can make. Nature brings its own versions. In environmental management, funding under {{ref:nature-mkt-092}} faces trade-offs among biodiversity conservation, carbon storage and fair distribution, since maximizing one reduces the other two. More broadly, the tension between prosperity for all and environmental conservation makes trade-offs necessary in sustainability.

nature-econ-095.title: Opportunity cost: the price of the road not taken
nature-econ-095.text: An hour away from work to buy $200 of office supplies costs more than $200. Someone who earns $25 an hour also gives up $25 of earnings. The $200 is paid out of pocket; the lost $25 is hidden but just as real. Together they show opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up when limited resources force you to pick one option over others. Put simply, it is the benefit you would have had from your second-best choice. The idea expresses the link between scarcity and choice, and its aim is the efficient use of scarce resources. It counts every cost of a decision, visible and hidden, and is not limited to money. Lost time, pleasure or any useful benefit counts too. One kind of cost is left out. Money already spent and unrecoverable should not sway present or future decisions (see {{ref:nature-econ-148}}). The concept also explains trade. A party that can produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others holds the edge described in {{ref:nature-econ-106}}. Governments face the same arithmetic: $840 billion spent on a war cannot fund healthcare, education or tax cuts.

nature-econ-098.title: Rational choice: people as careful calculators
nature-econ-098.text: Economists often explain behavior by asking a simple question: what would a rational person do, weighing the same costs and benefits? That is rational choice modeling. It assumes people can rank and weigh their options, so they choose by balancing costs against benefits. Their preferences are taken to be complete and transitive, and a decision counts as rational if it follows logically from them. Early neoclassical economists such as Jevons assumed people choose to maximize their happiness, or utility. The model can even show how individually rational people reach collectively irrational outcomes. Its critics are many. Herbert Simon argued that people's reasoning has limits ({{ref:nature-econ-022}}), so they often settle for a good-enough decision ({{ref:nature-econ-071}}). Research in behavioral psychology has challenged the theory and produced an alternative, {{ref:nature-econ-067}}. Others argue that people often act from habit, impulse or emotion rather than calculation. Economists, psychologists and sociologists have long disputed both its assumptions and its predictions.

nature-econ-102.title: The budget constraint: what your money can buy
nature-econ-102.text: Income draws a hard edge around every shopping list. A budget constraint is the full set of combinations of things a person can afford with their income at current prices. With two goods it becomes a straight line, the budget line, which shows the trade-off between them. Its slope is the ratio of the two prices. That ratio is the opportunity cost of one more unit of one good, measured in units of the other. Paired with indifference curves, the budget constraint is the basic tool for analyzing how consumers choose. The best affordable bundle usually lies where an indifference curve just touches the budget line. Real budgets are rarely so tidy. Taxes, subsidies, quantity discounts and welfare benefits can bend the line or put kinks in it. The idea applies to time as well. In labor economics the wage acts as the price of leisure, because one more hour off costs one hour's wage.

nature-econ-110.title: Consumer choice: how preferences become spending
nature-econ-110.text: Every shopping trip is, in theory, a small problem in getting the most for your money. Consumer choice theory is the part of microeconomics that explains how people's preferences shape what they spend and how much they demand. Its central assumption is that consumers maximize utility subject to their budget constraint, choosing the best bundle they can afford. Preferences are drawn as indifference curves, each showing bundles that leave the consumer equally satisfied. In practice, income, culture, product information and psychological factors all affect how people value goods. The theory makes one neat prediction: every price change splits into two parts, explained in {{ref:nature-econ-111}} and {{ref:nature-econ-147}}. Behavioral economists criticize the theory because consumers often rely on rough shortcuts that ignore some information ({{ref:nature-econ-054}}). People also let money already spent sway them, like traveling through a storm to use a concert ticket.

nature-econ-147.title: The substitution effect: switching to what got cheaper
nature-econ-147.text: When one good gets cheaper relative to another, buyers shift toward it. The substitution effect is that change in what a consumer buys, caused purely by the change in relative prices. Any price change can be split into this effect and a second one, {{ref:nature-econ-111}}, which comes from the change in purchasing power. On a graph, the substitution effect is a move along the original indifference curve, while the second effect is the move to a different curve. John Hicks and R. G. D. Allen introduced the idea to English readers in 1934, building on Pareto. They reached conclusions that Eugen Slutsky had found in 1915. A related measure, defined by Hicks and by Joan Robinson, tracks how the mix of inputs used shifts as their relative prices change.

nature-econ-150.title: The utility maximization problem: the best you can afford
nature-econ-150.text: In the textbook picture, every consumer solves the same puzzle. The utility maximization problem describes how a consumer chooses the most preferred bundle of goods they can afford with limited income at given prices. It assumes the consumer can rank every possible bundle by the utility it gives. Solving it gives a systematic account of what consumers buy and how that changes when income or prices change. The limit reflects scarcity, and money is not the only one: consumers may also face time constraints and budgets spread over time. One result is tidy. If all prices and income rise at the same rate, the affordable set and the best choice stay the same. Real consumers fall short. Lacking time or information, they sometimes pick bundles that do not maximize utility. The problem was first developed by the utilitarian philosophers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

nature-econ-137.title: Market structure: from many sellers to just one
nature-econ-137.text: How prices form in a market depends on its structure. That means how many firms sell in it, how alike their products are and how easily firms can enter or leave. At one extreme sits {{ref:nature-econ-353}}. Many small firms sell identical products and are price takers, unable to set their own price, which drives prices down to the cost of making one more unit. In {{ref:nature-econ-311}}, many firms sell slightly different products, as with restaurants, cereal and clothing. Next comes {{ref:nature-econ-364}}, where a few firms dominate. They may collude and form price-raising alliances ({{ref:nature-econ-301}}). At the other extreme is {{ref:nature-econ-349}}, a single supplier, which tends to charge higher prices and produce below the socially best level. The buyer's side has its own extreme, {{ref:nature-econ-377}}, with only one buyer. A mining company that is the only employer in an isolated town is an example, and it can set wages low.

nature-econ-128.title: Thinking at the margin: one more unit at a time
nature-econ-128.text: Economic decisions, in theory, are made one extra unit at a time. In economics, the margin is the current level of consumption or production. Marginal concepts describe what happens with one small change in that quantity rather than with the total. Whether to get one more unit depends on the benefit of that unit. A consumer keeps buying until the benefit of one more unit equals its market price. A firm facing a competitive market price keeps producing until one more unit would cost more than it sells for. These ideas form the basis of price theory and predict how much people buy and sell. Neoclassical analysis often assumes goods can be divided endlessly, so a marginal change can be infinitely small. Strictly, the smallest relevant step may be quite large. Marginal thinking matters for nature too. Economists generally agree on one rule for regulating emissions efficiently. Every polluter should face the full marginal social cost of its actions. {{ref:nature-pol-253}} uses the same logic, letting reductions happen first where cutting emissions is cheapest.

nature-econ-091.title: Marginal utility: the value of the next piece
nature-econ-091.text: Economists care less about the whole box of chocolates than about the next piece. Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction a person gets from consuming one more unit of a good or service. In economics, marginal means a small change from some starting level. Marginal utility can be positive, negative or zero. Negative means each extra unit does more harm than good. The concept underpins marginal analysis, which compares the extra benefits of an activity with its extra costs. Since utility is hard to measure directly, economists rank options by watching what people actually choose. The idea grew out of an old puzzle: how are prices set? Economists developed marginal utility while trying to explain it, and Daniel Bernoulli published the first clear statement of the theory in 1738. Critics note that people may not optimize as the theory assumes, and that utility varies between people and over time.

nature-econ-129.title: The marginal rate of substitution: what you would swap
nature-econ-129.text: Suppose a consumer would give up 2 units of one good to get 1 more unit of another, and feel exactly as satisfied. That swap rate, 2, is the marginal rate of substitution. Graphically it is the slope of an indifference curve at a given bundle, taken as a positive number, so it differs at each point on the curve. It also equals the marginal utility of the first good divided by the marginal utility of the second. A law of diminishing marginal rate of substitution follows. The more of one good a consumer already has, the less of the other they will give up for an extra unit. Two rules follow. Utility is highest when spending is split so that the marginal utility per unit of money is equal for every good. And two people keep trading as long as their swap rates differ. Once the rates are equal, no further exchange can benefit both.

nature-econ-131.title: Marginalism: why diamonds cost more than water
nature-econ-131.text: Water keeps people alive, yet diamonds cost more. Marginalism resolves the puzzle. It is the economic theory that explains differences in the value of goods by their marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit. Water has greater total utility, but a diamond has greater marginal utility. Behind this sits a law, also called Gossen's First Law, that each added unit brings less extra benefit than the one before (see {{ref:nature-econ-092}}). Marginalism explains prices through the meeting of buyers and sellers: buyers want less and sellers offer more as the price rises. Following Alfred Marshall, marginalists also explained costs by the extra output each added input produces. At the most general level, the extra cost of one more unit is an opportunity cost, though the term usually means the extra money spent. Marginalism is an integral part of mainstream economic theory.

nature-hist-023.title: Neoclassical economics: the mainstream's core
nature-hist-023.text: The dominant approach to microeconomics takes its name from Thorstein Veblen, who coined the term in 1900. Neoclassical economics explains production, consumption and prices through {{ref:nature-econ-360}}, driven by people maximizing utility and firms maximizing profit. Three assumptions hold it up. People have rational preferences. Individuals maximize utility and firms maximize profits. And people act independently with full information. In this view a good's value comes from its marginal utility to the user, unlike {{ref:nature-hist-012}} and Marxian economics, which use the labor theory of value. The approach developed in the 1870s and replaced the classical school as the mainstream. Its break with the classical school is often dated to Jevons and Menger in 1871 and Walras in 1874–1877. From the 1950s, combined with Keynes's ideas, it formed the neoclassical synthesis that dominated mainstream economics. Although it favors markets, it accepts that externalities, a form of market failure, can stop markets from producing socially desirable outcomes. Under suitable assumptions, though, flexible prices allow every welfare-improving trade, so markets left free yield an optimum of social welfare.

openers.econ: Economics begins with a person choosing. Economists measure how satisfied that person is with a state of the world and call it utility, and they call anything that gives welfare or satisfaction a good. Microeconomics then asks how individuals and firms decide to use scarce resources, and how their choices interact. This part builds that toolkit from the ground up, because every later question about what nature is worth depends on what economists mean by value.
openers.choices-scarcity-and-value: Why does anyone choose one thing over another? Economists answer with the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, and with utility, a measure of how satisfied each option leaves them. To study one change at a time, they build models, simplified pictures of an economic process, and assume everything else stays equal. This chapter also separates two kinds of claim: statements about how the economy works, and judgments about what people or societies ought to do.
